content: Women with a history of vascular disease, end-organ damage, or diabetes mellitus lasting more than 20 years should be carefully evaluated before initiating therapy. Similarly, individuals with inherited or acquired hypercoagulopathies, smokers over the age of 35, or those with renal insufficiency, hepatic dysfunction, or adrenal insufficiency are at increased risk and require special consideration. Patients experiencing headaches with focal neurological symptoms or migraines with aura should avoid therapy, as these conditions may increase the risk of stroke. Women over 35 years of age with any type of migraine headache are also at heightened risk. Smoking more than 15 cigarettes per day at age 35 or older significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular complications. Major surgeries requiring prolonged immobilization elevate the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Women with a history of cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, whether current or past, should not use this therapy. Thrombogenic rhythm disorders and hereditary or acquired thrombophilias are contraindications as well. Additionally, women with endometrial carcinoma or other estrogen-dependent neoplasms, whether confirmed or suspected, should avoid therapy. Unexplained abnormal vaginal or uterine bleeding must be investigated before initiating therapy. Women with a history of cholestatic jaundice during pregnancy or jaundice related to prior contraceptive use should not use this therapy. Those receiving hepatitis C drug combinations containing ombitasvir, paritaprevir, ritonavir (with or without dasabuvir) should discontinue therapy during treatment and may resume approximately two weeks after completing the hepatitis C regimen. Acute viral hepatitis or severe (decompensated) cirrhosis of the liver are contraindications. Before starting therapy, a thorough evaluation of personal and family history of thrombotic or thromboembolic disorders is essential. Therapy is contraindicated in women with a high risk of arterial or venous thrombotic events. Caution is advised in patients with a family history of breast cancer, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), or both, as well as those with current or previous depression, endometriosis, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, bone mineral density changes, renal or hepatic impairment, bone metabolic disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Conditions exacerbated by fluid retention, such as migraines, asthma, or epilepsy, should also be considered. The risk of VTE is highest during the first year of combined oral contraceptive (COC) use and when restarting after a break of four weeks or longer. The risk of thromboembolic disease gradually diminishes after discontinuing COCs. However, COCs increase the risk of arterial thrombosis, which can lead to strokes and myocardial infarctions, particularly in women with other risk factors. COCs have been shown to increase both relative and attributable risks of cerebrovascular events, including thrombotic and hemorrhagic strokes. This risk is especially pronounced in women over 35 years of age who smoke. Underlying risk factors for cardiovascular disease or VTE, such as hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and obesity, should be carefully assessed before initiating therapy, particularly in women over 35 years of age. Therapy should be discontinued if an arterial thrombotic event or VTE occurs. If feasible, therapy should be stopped at least four weeks before and through two weeks after major surgery or surgeries associated with an elevated risk of VTE, as well as during and following prolonged immobilization. Therapy should not be initiated earlier than four weeks postpartum in women who are not breastfeeding. The risk of postpartum VTE decreases after the third postpartum week, while the risk of ovulation increases. Therapy should be discontinued if jaundice, visual problems (such as contact lens intolerance), signs of VTE, unusually severe migraines, significant blood pressure increases, or severe depression develop. Therapy should also be stopped four weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization. Women receiving hepatitis C drug combinations containing ombitasvir, paritaprevir, ritonavir (with or without dasabuvir) should discontinue therapy during treatment and may restart approximately two weeks after completing the regimen. The estrogen component of COCs may increase serum concentrations of thyroxine-binding globulin, sex hormone-binding globulin, and cortisol-binding globulin. This may necessitate an increase in the dose of replacement thyroid hormone or cortisol therapy. Long-term use of oral contraceptives (≥5 years) may be associated with an increased risk of liver cancer, with the risk increasing with the duration of use. Oral contraceptives may also increase the risk of cervical cancer, although human papillomavirus (HPV) remains the primary risk factor for this cancer. Women with hereditary angioedema may experience exacerbation of symptoms due to exogenous estrogens. Chloasma may occasionally occur, particularly in women with a history of chloasma gravidarum. Women prone to chloasma should avoid sun or ultraviolet radiation exposure while receiving therapy. Oral contraceptives have been shown to increase the risk of cerebrovascular events, including thrombotic and hemorrhagic strokes, particularly in older women (>35 years) who are hypertensive and smoke. Women with liver disease, such as acute viral hepatitis or severe cirrhosis, should not use COCs. Acute or chronic liver function disturbances may necessitate discontinuation of COCs until liver function markers return to normal and COC causation is excluded. Therapy should be discontinued if jaundice develops. Certain conditions, such as smoking and migraines without aura, which do not contraindicate COC use in younger women, are contraindications in women over 35 years of age. Women with migraines, particularly those with aura or focal neurological symptoms, are at increased risk of stroke when taking COCs. A positive association has been observed between the amount of estrogen and progestogen in COCs and the risk of vascular disease. A decline in serum high-density lipoproteins (HDL) has been reported with many progestational agents, which is associated with an increased incidence of ischemic heart disease. Women being treated for hyperlipidemias should be closely monitored if they elect to use oral contraceptives. Some progestogens may elevate LDL levels, making hyperlipidemia management more challenging. Nonhormonal contraception should be considered in women with uncontrolled dyslipidemias. Persistent hypertriglyceridemia may occur, and elevations in plasma triglycerides may lead to pancreatitis and other complications. Diarrhea and/or vomiting may reduce hormone absorption, leading to decreased serum concentrations. Blood pressure increases have been reported in women taking oral contraceptives, particularly in older users and with continued use. Women with a history of hypertension or hypertension-related diseases, or renal disease, should be encouraged to use alternative contraception methods. If women with hypertension choose to use oral contraceptives, they should be closely monitored, and therapy should be discontinued if significant blood pressure elevation occurs. The onset or worsening of migraines, or the development of a new headache pattern that is recurrent, persistent, or severe, requires discontinuation of oral contraceptives and evaluation of the cause. The convenience of having no scheduled menstrual bleeding should be weighed against the inconvenience of unscheduled breakthrough bleeding and spotting. Ectopic and intrauterine pregnancies may occur in cases of contraceptive failure. Women with a strong family history of breast cancer or breast nodules should be monitored with particular care. For women with well-controlled hypertension, blood pressure should be monitored, and treatment should be stopped if blood pressure rises significantly. Studies suggest a small increased relative risk of developing gallbladder disease among COC users. COCs may worsen existing gallbladder disease, and a history of COC-related cholestasis predicts an increased risk with subsequent use. Women with a history of pregnancy-related cholestasis may also be at increased risk for COC-related cholestasis. If a woman develops new headaches that are recurrent, persistent, or severe, the cause should be evaluated, and therapy discontinued if indicated. Consider discontinuation if there is an increased frequency or severity of migraines during COC use, as this may be prodromal to a cerebrovascular event. If bleeding persists or occurs after previously regular cycles, investigate causes such as pregnancy or malignancy. If pathology and pregnancy are excluded, bleeding irregularities may resolve over time or with a change to a different contraceptive product. Women receiving therapy may experience amenorrhea or absence of withdrawal bleeding, even if they are not pregnant. If scheduled withdrawal bleeding does not occur, consider the possibility of pregnancy if the patient has not adhered to the prescribed dosing schedule. If pregnancy is confirmed, discontinue oral contraceptive use. Contraceptive hormones and/or metabolites are present in human milk. COCs can reduce milk production in breastfeeding women, particularly before breastfeeding is well-established. When possible, advise nursing women to use alternative contraception methods until they discontinue breastfeeding. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered alongside the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who have used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy. Studies also do not suggest a teratogenic effect when taken inadvertently during early pregnancy. Oral contraceptives should not be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. For any patient who has missed two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing oral contraceptive use. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule, consider the possibility of pregnancy at the time of the first missed period. Oral contraceptive use should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed.
